paragraphs.heading: A solid without a pattern
paragraphs.text: An amorphous solid is a solid without the long-range order that marks a crystal. The name comes from Greek words meaning without shape or form. Glasses, metallic glasses, and some plastics and polymers are all examples. People sometimes use the word glass to mean the same thing, but strictly a glass is an amorphous material that goes through a glass transition.

paragraphs.heading: Order up close
paragraphs.text: The atoms are not simply random. Up close, amorphous materials are built from small blocks that can resemble the basic units of the crystal form of the same compound, a local order that comes from chemical bonding. Short-range order reaches only to an atom's nearest neighbours, usually 1-2 atomic spacings, and medium-range order can extend 1-2 nm beyond that. What is missing is regularity over long distances: no small unit, repeated over and over, can describe the whole material.

paragraphs.heading: An open problem in physics
paragraphs.text: How a liquid freezes into an amorphous solid, the glass transition, is counted among the important unsolved problems of physics. There are several theoretical models, yet neither the glass transition nor the behaviour of glassy solids at low temperatures is well understood at a basic level. Researchers in condensed matter physics study these materials both at the high temperatures of the glass transition and near absolute zero.

paragraphs.heading: Strange behaviour in the cold
paragraphs.text: At very low temperatures, below 1-10 K, many amorphous solids share similar properties. Detailed experiments since the 1970s show that their specific heat rises almost in a straight line with temperature, while their thermal conductivity rises nearly with its square. These traits are called anomalous because crystals behave very differently. A model based on tunnelling two-level systems describes many of them, but after more than 50 years there is still no microscopic theory.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to see inside
paragraphs.text: Working out the structure of an amorphous solid is difficult. Standard crystallography methods often fall short because there is no long-range order. Where crystals give strong Bragg diffraction, amorphous materials give broad, diffuse peaks, so extra analysis is needed to pull out real structural detail. It helps to gather data from both X-rays and neutrons, which scatter differently and so fill in each other's gaps.

paragraphs.heading: Tools that help
paragraphs.text: Pair distribution function analysis uses diffraction data to find the chance of two atoms sitting a given distance apart, which reveals local order. Atomic electron tomography takes 2D images at many tilt angles inside a transmission electron microscope and rebuilds them into a 3D picture of where each kind of atom sits. Computer methods such as molecular dynamics and density functional theory are often combined with these experiments.
